probe: journalctl answers a bounded newest-first read here. The group is the whole of the question: journalctl on PATH is not the answer, because an unprivileged reader is served its own uid's entries and nothing else — measured on the lab guest, 200 of 200 entries came back _UID=1000 with no kernel transport at all — so a probe that only looked for the binary would report yes for a collector that can see one user's session and calls it the machine's journal.

collections.name: journal

rules.sentence: Entry logged at priority 2 or below; emerg, alert and crit are trusted as severity from the priority alone.
Entry logged at err by a container: the journald log driver maps a container's stderr to err, so the priority is the stream it was written on, not a severity the application chose.
Entry logged at err. err alone is not attention-worthy — applications log routine output at err — so this entry is recorded, not judged.
This message identity repeats within the page this entry was read from: repetition is the signal priority cannot give — judge it by content, not by level.

collections.question: what has this machine logged, newest first?

Message.sentence: The log line as its emitter wrote it. Content, and the widest disclosure surface this product has: a message is whatever a program chose to print, which on some machine somewhere includes a path, an address or a credential. Declared `string` because that is what journald carries for a text entry; an entry whose bytes are not valid UTF-8 is rendered by journalctl as an array of byte values and republished here unchanged, which the declared type cannot express and the vocabulary has no union for.

MessageId.sentence: The emitter's own catalogue id for a message TYPE, so two entries differing only in an interpolated value share it. It is a constant compiled into the emitting software — the same 32 hex digits on every machine running it — and most emitters set none, which is why repetition falls back to the message text.

Priority.sentence: The syslog severity, 0 (emerg) to 7 (debug). Parsed to an integer rather than republished as the string journald spells it, because it is the one field this product compares numerically; everything else keeps the journal's own spelling.

SyslogIdentifier.sentence: What the emitter called itself — the tag a person reads first when scanning a log. Software's own name for itself, identical on every machine running it.

Transport.sentence: Which stream the entry arrived on, as journald recorded it. It is what distinguishes 'the application said this is an error' from 'the application wrote to stderr': the journald log driver maps a container's stderr to priority err, and that mapping is the single biggest source of misleading err entries.

SystemdUnit.sentence: The system unit the emitting process belonged to, attached by journald rather than claimed by the process. A kernel entry has none, because no unit emitted it.

SystemdUserUnit.sentence: The user unit the emitting process belonged to, where a per-user systemd manager was running. Present on the same entries SystemdUnit names user@<uid>.service for, and on no others.

Container.sentence: The container that emitted this entry, as the journald log driver labelled it. Content, because a container name is a word somebody chose. Its presence is also what makes a priority-3 entry readable: it says the err may be the stream the line arrived on rather than a severity the application picked.

Command.sentence: The emitting process's command name — the fifteen-character comm the kernel holds, not its full argv. Software's own name for itself.

PID.sentence: The emitting process's id, republished as the string journald spells it. A string rather than an integer on purpose: journald renders every field as text and this collection converts exactly one of them, so PID travels as it was written and a consumer that wants arithmetic parses it knowingly.

Timestamp.sentence: When journald recorded the entry, to the second, in UTC. Derived from the journal's microsecond realtime stamp; an entry whose stamp is zero or the unset u64 carries no Timestamp at all, because a manufactured epoch is worse than an admitted absence.

RepeatCount.sentence: How many entries in THIS page share this message's identity — its catalogue id where it has one, its text where it does not. Repetition is the signal priority cannot give: it answers 'is this line spam', which no single record can, and it is scoped to the page rather than to the entry because a window is the only thing a count can be taken over.

RepeatWindow.sentence: How many entries the page RepeatCount was counted over. It rides beside the count because a count without its window is unreadable — three in three is every line, three in a thousand is noise — and both are properties of the read rather than of the entry.

collections.redaction_exemption: This collector serves no evidence verb yet (DESIGN 18's partial-verb ruling), so there is no raw payload to withhold paths from — and when it does, the withholding cannot be a path list, which is why the exemption says so now rather than being written as one later. A journal entry's credential surface is not AT a path: it is INSIDE MESSAGE, in text a program chose, and no path expression names half of a sentence. The two facts declared `content` above (Message, Container) are the whole of that surface, they are declared as such so a policy can act on them (DESIGN 21), and an evidence verb here will have to redact by rule rather than by path or not ship.

reference_commands.purpose: the same page this collection reads, by hand
one entry again, addressed by the cursor this collection names it with
the same page a person reads, to check a rendering against the fields
